speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Minister of Finance and the government launched a vicious attack on workers across Canada by imposing a 3 per cent cap on Public Service wage increases. They have told every employer in Canada that it is okay to throw away the right to bargain, it is okay to threaten workers with job losses and contracting out. If all that does not work, the government is prepared to interfere with conciliation and arbitration and force workers back to the job.
Workers in every community across Canada will suffer from this cynical severe attack on the hard won rights of workers. When 1.3 million Canadians are out of work, taking purchasing power away from consumers only guarantees that suffering will be even deeper and more prolonged.
The Minister of Finance has told working people they are going to have to swallow the devastating affects of his high interest rate policy, his high dollar policy and his high unemployment policy. They are going to pay twice for the GST) once at the cash register and next in their pay cheques.
Workers in Canada are not going to savage each other to survive, they are going to savage this government.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday, as Iraqi troops withdrew from Kuwait, pursuant to UN resolution 660, coalition aircraft, including huge American B-52 bombers, dropped cluster bombs and 1,000-pound bombs on the fleeing troops. U.S. airmen said: "We hit the jackpot. It looks like the Iraqis are moving out and we are hitting them hard. It is not going to take too many days before there is nothing left of them."
The Prime Minister, exercising what former UN ambassador Stephen Lewis has described as poodle diplomacy, has refused to state what role Canadian CF-18s are playing in this carnage.
Today, Foreign Minister Tariq Aziz stated that Iraq accepts all relevant UN resolutions. It is now clearer than ever that the U.S. is determined to press on far beyond any UN resolution to achieve their agenda of the total destruction of Iraq's military, political and economic structure.
When will our Prime Minister finally show some independence and tell George Bush that enough is enough, this mad war must stop and that Canada will no longer be part of the killing machine.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance is to be congratulated for setting a clear course for recession recovery and the restoration of economic growth and renewed prosperity.
I, for one, was brought up to believe you have to pay your bills and I am sure most Canadians believe their government should do the same thing. The government can serve Canadians best by bringing inflation and interest rates under control. A strong economy is the best road to full employment and prosperity for Canadians. I commend the Minister of Finance for leading the way by freezing his own salary, and I am sure all members will join me in agreeing to the cap on our salaries. It is only reasonable that we should be joined in this restraint by our fellow employees in the Public Service.

February 27, 1991
The continued cap in growth of EPF payments sends a strong message to the provinces that they too are part of the problem, thus must be part of the solution. The Minister of Finance has set a solid course. Let us all get behind him with our full support.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday's Tory Budget completely forgot Montreal. In Montreal, the unemployment rate is now 13.4 per cent. The government has made cuts in unemployment insurance, the job development program, social housing, medicare and payments to the provinces.

In a report dated February 4, Statistics Canada said that Montreal had more poverty than any other city in Canada. Twenty two per cent of the residents of greater Montreal live below the poverty level compared to 13 per cent in Toronto. And what is the Conservative government's answer? "Too bad, boys, get help somewhere else. We can find $1 billion for a war in Iraq but we cannot find money for housing, hospitals and jobs at home." God bless Canada.
This government was so intimidated by the headlinegrabbing protests over last spring's budget proposals to eliminate women's centres funding that it now hides behind the thin veil of ministerial consultation. Canadians are not fooled. They demand to know who is being targeted and why.

Mr. Speaker, I was glad to see that in the 1991 Budget, program expenditures will increase by $7.5 billion in 1991-92, and also that the 6.9 per cent increase over the previous fiscal year will go to where needs are most pressing, i.e. $3 billion for assistance to the unemployed, $1.6 billion for the elderly, $1.3 billion for farmers in difficulty, $600 million to support our troops in the gulf and $1 billion for all other programs.
Mr. Speaker, for the sale of equity, the disability tax credit will be increased by $125 from 575 to $700 as of the 1991 taxation year. This means that federal assistance to disabled Canadians will increase by $35 million per year.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today on behalf of all Canadians to demand honesty from this government.
Yesterday, the finance minister announced his plan to slash $75 million this year, and $125 million every year thereafter, from groups working for equality and social justice. But his government has refused to tell Canadians from where those amounts are being taken. Nor will it tell us in the estimates, the traditional forum for revealing the victims of this kind of budget slashing.
What should Canadians make of their government's spineless secretiveness? There is only one conclusion, Mr. Speaker. This government plans to knock off equality-seeking groups one at a time in order to escape organized opposition.

Mr. Speaker, a headline to a newspaper article reads:
"U.S. firms warned Canada's GST to hurt them".
American companies should wake up and smell the GST, says a U.S. tax expert.
"I think American companies are going to be the big losers under the goods and services tax", said Cliff Massa, a Washington lawyer who specializes in value-added taxes.
Now largely ignored by U.S. firms, the seven-per-cent GST will make Canadian competitors more efficient.
"I do not know why companies here seem so disinterested."
Massa, who has been sounding the GST alarm in the United States for the past year, said Canada's old federal sales tax was a boon to U.S. companies.
"I think everybody understands (the federal sales tax) discriminated against the Canadian manufacturer."

February 27, 1991

"It has both amazed and frustrated me, in that I don't think
Americans have been paying any attention to the GST," said Massa.

Mr. Speaker, the budget stands as the last will and testament of medicare. It is impossible to conceive the government can surrender its bargaining power of transfer payments and still keep provinces from bolting from the national health care system.
Provinces are being forced to close hospital beds. Deaths occur while waiting for surgery.
This budget will create a two-tier system of health care. Where you live and what you earn will determine your status in the system.
And who will suffer the most? The struggling middle class, the seniors and the poor.
Health care is a fundamental right of Canadian citizenship and now the government is destroying this right. For six years this government has failed to enforce the Canada Health Act. Now we are asked to believe national health standards will be upheld with new legislation.
We do not need new legislation to save us from user fees and extra billing. What we need is a new government.

Mr. Speaker, recently the United States imposed a restriction on Canadian seed potatoes because there were reported cases of potatoes being contaminated with the plant killing virus PVY-N.
The Department of Agriculture has indicated that the infected areas have been clearly identified and the spread of the virus has been confined, ensuring the successful eradication of the disease.
New Brunswick seed potatoes received a virtual clean bill of health as a result of the various tests.
As a result, the Americans amended their restrictions and are now allowing New Brunswick potatoes to cross
the border. However, the Americans continue to have stringent controls on P.E.I. potatoes. The lesson for Canada is simply this, that we must ensure top quality products only are exported out of our country into neighbouring countries to ensure quality.

Mr. Speaker, my constituents in Haldimand-Norfolk were shocked and dismayed at the callous attack the Minister of Finance took on the tobacco farmers and communities of my area.
Did the minister have any idea of the economic hardship that the people of Haldimand-Norfolk have been going through because of his economic mismanagement?
Did he have any idea that the implementation of this tobacco tax would push many of my constituents over the edge into bankruptcy?
Even though the minister collects over $5 billion a year with this tobacco tax, less than $10 million of that is returned to the farmers whose livelihoods depend on it.
Did the minister not know what the impact of his budget would have on the communities and the small entrepreneurs surrounding the tobacco belt?
Did the minister not know that there is anger and frustration and that people are desolate and, in some cases, without hope, and that they are taking this frustration out on themselves and, in some cases, on one another.
Tbbacco farmers have subsidized the minister's programs long enough. It is time the minister put his money where his mouth is and either buy tobacco farmers out of give them the long-term certainty that they need to survive.

Mr. Speaker, following a budget there is always an outcry from those free spenders who feel the government has unlimited resources. We are hearing this chorus again today, but we are not hearing it from the average Canadian, the taxpayer, the person who pays the bills.

February 27, 1991
Our taxpayers have had it with government spending and this budget gives them hope.
The Minister of Finance has listened to those who demand that government operate in a more fiscally responsible manner. Business cannot survive if it overspends and neither can our country.
Committing all GST revenue to the debt servicing and reduction fund is a positive step. Canadians do not like taxes and appreciate the legislated assurance that GST revenues will go toward debt reduction and not new spending.
For the first time, we will put a ceiling on how much politicians can spend. My Private Members' Motion No. 684 asks for this and I am pleased to see it included in the budget.
The country faces difficult times and the minister has chosen to make tough decisions and thinking Canadians are going to support him.

Mr. Speaker, the champagne bottles were popping all night in the boardrooms of The Business Council on National Issues and the Prime Minister's friends.
Unscathed in their tax shelters, big business has been toasting their beloved Minister of Finance. He has relentlessly unleashed devastating fiscal bombs on the working poor and middle class Canadians.
Budget damage assessment will show that he has inflicted severe hardships on just about everybody except his cronies, the 150 members of the BCNI-and the deficit.
The Minister of Finance said last night and I quote:
I have heard the anguish of people who have lost their jobs or
their businesses.
Yet, while the unemployed line up at the food banks, I can only hear Tom d'Aquino and his gang clinking the glasses of their tax-deductible cocktails.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to commend the finance minister on the new tax measures he has introduced to assist disabled persons.
Last June, the Standing Committee on Human Rights and Status of Disabled Persons chaired by our colleague, the hon. member for Oxford, tabled a report calling on the government to make the economic integration of disabled persons a national priority.
The important new steps taken in yesterday's budget constitute one element of this strategy to promote equal opportunities for Canadians with disabilities.
They build on an impressive series of initiatives to improve the quality of life of Canadians with disabilities and remove barriers to their full participation in our society.
By assisting both employers and employees, these new tax measures will help ensure that disabled Canadians have equal opportunity to participate in the workforce.

With the Tories' cut of $28 million to Telefilm Canada, Canadian film makers will be singing the Bye, Bye Blues.
Since this government entered into close trade relations with the Americans, Canada's film industry has suffered from the divided loyalties. The government first cut the tax incentive program for film and video production which was $200 million yearly.
Then it failed to produce distribution legislation to increase the number of Canadian films on our screens to 3 per cent against its own task force recommendations and promises but close to the heart of the finance minister's American cousin, Jack Valenti.
Not only could the Telefilm freeze impact on the feature film industry, but it also could become une histoire inventee for the CBC as it receives about $31 million yearly from the broadcast fund.
It is clear to this side of the House that this government is editing its film policy and determined to leave the Canadian film industry on the cutting room floor.
Mr. Speaker, let's get one thing clear.
Oh, oh.

Canadian consumers did not cause this recession. World stock markets did not cause this recession. The Persian Gulf crisis did not cause the recession.
If the Minister of Finance wants to know who caused the recession, he should buy a mirror, pay the GST and look in it because he made this recession.
I ask the Prime Minister why, in this time of recession, he allowed the Minister of Finance to cut social and job programs at a time of devastating unemployment. Why did he allow the Minister of Finance to cut housing programs at a time when emergency shelters are bursting at the seams?
Why did the Prime Minister approve a budget which attacked the victims of the very recession he and his government created?

Mr. Speaker, I might remind the hon. member of something that she said about a year or so ago.
She said: "We face the danger point with the deficit." She went on to say: "I think it is important for any leadership candidate to go to the countiy and to preach fiscal sanity."
More, more.

I would also draw to her attention comments that were made yesterday by representatives of the provincial government that is the greatest amount in debt and the one that is facing the same type of problem that we are in the federal government.
Mr. Hubert Kitchen, the Minister of Finance of the province of Newfoundland, said: "Mr. Wilson's budget is quite a responsible one given the times in which we live and given the essential importance of all governments in Canada of living within their means. I think he has made
Oral Questions
a sincere attempt at that. I think we should give him credit for attempting to do better."
Hear, hear.

This is the essential choice that Canadians face. We either live within our means, or we move to the approach that the hon. member is suggesting that we take of saying: "Let's forget about fiscal sanity," to use the words that she used last March.
We must realize that we had been running, until 1984, government spending far too quickly, averaging 13.8 per cent per annum. It is important that Canadians and the hon. member for Hamilton East understand the significance of this budget in getting us back to fiscal sanity.

Mr. Speaker, his interest rate policies have failed. His employment policies have failed. His tax policies have failed. This is a minister who is not in a position to talk about fiscal sanity.
Could the Prime Minister explain why he is allowing the Minister of Finance to destroy our country's system of universal medicare? How can the Prime Minister pretend, on the one hand, to support universal medicare and then destroy funding for it? How can the Prime Minister tear the heart out of our health care system at a time when the very nature of the country depends upon the hallmark of decency and caring that is reflected in our health care system?

speakeroldname: Hon. Perrin Beatty (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, how soon former Liberal leadership candidates forget what they once said.
According to the Manitoba Dauphin Herald, when the hon. member opposite was running for the leadership of the Liberal Party, she said this: "Copps said if she is Liberal leader and Prime Minister, she will reform the income tax system and cut government spending instead of imposing a tax".
How soon they forget.
What threatens the social programs that are important to Canadians is the fact that out of every dollar that goes to Ottawa in tax revenues, the first 35 cents goes just to pay the interest on the national debt. That means that each Canadian, every man, woman and child in this countiy, has a debt in Ottawa of over $15,000.

February 27, 1991
Oral Questions
How much higher is the hon. member prepared to see that go, or will she be honest with Canadians and say that it is time that this generation started to pay its own way?

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister, who was supposed to be responsible for Canadian unity. He knows this Budget is not only anti-Quebec but anti-Canadian as well. The federal government is forcing the provinces to introduce user fees. It is forcing them to cut health care by cutting its health insurance program. The federal government cuts payments and still asks the provinces to provide the same services. Could the Prime Minister inform the House, at this difficult time in Canada's history, why he is attacking health insurance, the only program that unites Canadians in Quebec, Ontario, western Canada and the Maritimes? The only program in which all Canadians really believe? Is the Prime Minister going to tell us he is willing to sacrifice the health insurance program to the national debt?

speakeroldname: Hon. Perrin Beatty (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is not the first time that members opposite have taken the approach of trying to frighten the elderly, the sick and the poor. It is a tactic that is reprehensible. It was a tactic that was followed by them in the last election and was rejected by Canadians then. It will be rejected by Canadians now.
The federal government is not asking the provinces to do anything that the federal government is not prepared to do itself. Transfer payments to the provinces will go up by some 3.7 per cent, while spending on federal programs will be going up by 3.4 per cent. Mr. Speaker, if you look at the cost to the provinces, this amounts to less than one-half of 1 per cent of provincial revenues. And to suggest that this is the death-knell of medicare is simply Liberal scaremongering once again.
Hear, hear.

My question is for the Minister of Finance, who seems to enjoy quotations.
Back in 1982 when he wanted the job of presenting budgets, he said this: "The government must begin to realize that it is individual people who are being hurt. We cannot stay here in an ivory tower in Ottawa; we must deal with individual Canadians who are losing their jobs and their businesses."
Can the minister explain how a $100 million cutback to the Canadian Jobs Strategy and interest rates which he projects to be in excess of 10 per cent will help individual Canadians keep their jobs and businesses?

Mr. Speaker, I think my hon. friend should search a little longer for quotes, because I think he will find that consistently through all my time in government I have been cautioning about the growth of deficits and debt.
When we faced the preparation of this budget, we were looking at a budget deficit of $35 billion, which we have been able to bring down to a deficit of $30.5 billion.
What I am hearing from hon. members opposite is that they would want to increase that deficit from $35 billion to $36, $37, $38 billion. That is completely unacceptable. That would result in an increase in interest rates, and the people he is referring to in that quote he took of mine would be the first ones who would be hurt.
We have designed this budget to bring interest rates down. We are doing that through legislated controls on government spending, through getting the deficit down from where it would have been and getting it down even further next year, and by bringing in inflation controls, inflation targets, which are designed to bring interest rates down. That is the fundamental difference between the government on this side of the House and the Liberal Party on the other side of the House. We are going to bring down interest rates to ignite the economy. The Liberals on the other side would just spend their way into oblivion.
Hear, hear.
Mr. Speaker, the minister's problem is that he thinks deficits are about numbers. Deficits are also about people.

Hear, hear.
February 27, 1991

According to yesterday's Budget, even if economic recovery begins in the second half of this year, we will still have a million and a half unemployed in this country.
Mr. Speaker, I have another quote. The Minister of Finance also said, and I quote:

"When people are struggling for survival, when people fear that they will lose their jobs, there is not much trust".

In light of what he said, could the minister explain how his Budget could give a million and a half unemployed Canadians and their families any reason to trust the government?
Mr. Speaker, in the 15 years leading up to 1984, what we saw-
Oh, oh.
Mr. Speaker, I am going to show hon. members how this is veiy relevant to today.
You haven't been right on a prediction yet.

Mr. Speaker, in the 15 years up to 1984 government spending increased at 13.8 per cent per annum, year in and year out. According to Jeff Simpson this morning, he said: "Ottawa became a fiscal cripple in the years 1975 to 1984 when the federal government accumulated nearly $200 billion worth of debt".
The message here, which is totally lost on the Liberals on the other side of the House, is that choices they and we might want to make today have been taken away from us by the runaway spending during that time as the debt built up.
If hon. members do not understand that lesson of the past, they are living in another world.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. The Minister of Finance talks about choices. He talks about making these
Oral Questions
choices but not having any room to move. There are over 1.5 million Canadians who have no choice because they have no job.
I want to say to the Minister of Finance that certainly the Liberal government during the last recession also, I might add, capped old age pensions and family allowances, cut wages, put over a million Canadians out of work. At that time this Minister of Finance said to the then Liberal government: "Why is it that the Liberal government continues to take Canadians to the edge of a cliff and push some of them off?" That is what Canadians are asking this finance minister and this Conservative government.
My question to the finance minister is simply this: Why in this budget is there not any programs to get Canadians back working? That is the choice this minister should be giving Canadians, the choice of a job.

Mr. Speaker, unfortunately I have to say that my friend opposite totally misunderstands this budget. The essential objective of this budget is to get those Canadians that she is talking about back to work by bringing about lower interest rates. By bringing about lower interest rates we can give the greatest amount of stimulus to the economy that we can.
What I am hearing from my hon. friend is that she would take that $35 billion deficit we are starting with this year, sprinkle around money through all parts of the economy, build it up to about $37 billion or $38 billion. The result of that would be higher interest rates, which would totally overwhelm the limited benefits of that additional spending.
That is the direction we are going with this budget. It is designed through the spending caps, through the reduction in the deficit and the inflation targets to get interest rates down and to keep down in the broadest possible way.

I have a supplementary question, Mr. Speaker, for the Prime Minister.
The Minister of Finance says that creating 1.5 million unemployed is creating prosperity. When the interest rates were even higher, he told us we needed the high interest rates because that was going to be better for the economy. Now he tells us he is going to lower the interest rates with which we agree, but he still says we

Oral Questions
have to have over 1.5 million unemployed. This is totally unacceptable.
I want to ask the Prime Minister who, just two weeks ago, told Canadians in a major speech in Toronto that a major part of national unity was to continue the Canadian tradition of national standards and singled out health care and the environment in particular.
How can the Prime Minister seriously talk of national unity when this budget helps to destroy medicare, does not do anything for the environment and does not have any job creation at all? How can he speak of national unity when he cannot even provide jobs for Canadians?

Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend says that the Minister of Finance indicated that we must have 1.5 million people unemployed. That is a complete distortion. He never said any such thing, and I know that my hon. friend-
Oh, oh.

He never said any such thing and I know that my hon. friend at an appropriate time will want to rise and correct the impression that she has given because it is completely inaccurate.
In point of fact the figure of 1.5 million is, however, applicable because it is just about the number of new jobs created by this government since it was sworn in, in 1984. That job creating record was the best of all the OECD countries and led the G-7 with the exception of Japan.
We are now in a recession, which we have acknowledged. We are going to work our way out of it in the real world not by promises of some better day to come by spending borrowed money, but by getting interest rates down, re-energizing the private sector, attracting international investment, and creating durable jobs.

I have a supplementary question, Mr. Speaker, for the Minister of Finance.
There are many ways that the Minister of Finance can justify his budget, but it is the Minister of Finance who said that he projects 10 per cent unemployment. That means about 1.5 million Canadians unemployed. I am
not suggesting he likes it, but that is his projection and so he has projected a budget based on a high unemployment rate.
I want to ask the Minister of Finance another question.

In 1982, the current Secretary of State for External Affairs told the Liberal government that it was asking low and middle-income Canadians to shoulder more than their fair share of the burden. Yesterday, the Tory government made the same mistake. The disadvantaged and the middle class are still footing the bill.
My question is directed to the Minister of Finance. Why didn't the government decide to get rid of corporate tax loopholes in this Budget?

Mr. Speaker, I do not know how many times I have to say it to the hon. member. The essential purpose of corporate income tax reform was to close a number of the loopholes that she talked about and was quite correct back two or three years ago, but we have seen many of those loopholes closed. We have the banks, which at that time were paying no tax, paying about $1 billion worth of taxes this year.
We brought in the large corporations tax. That is covering all corporations that have capital over $10 million. We have seen in this last year where corporate profits have fallen by about 40 or 50 per cent, but corporate income tax revenues have only dropped about 5 per cent. Why? It is because they do not have the same loopholes that they had before. They have been closed by this government.
If she has any other loopholes she wants us to close, she should bring them to my attention. I would be very delighted to listen to them and respond if it is appropriate.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance.
February 27, 1991

The Minister of Finance in the province of Newfoundland may be impressed with this budget, but the people of Newfoundland and Labrador know that this is the mother of all budgets.
Hear, hear.

What we see is the Minister of Finance and his budget in full retreat in the face of the recession. This minister has forecast a 10 per cent unemployment rate, a 10 per cent unemployment rate at the same time that job strategy has been cut by $100 million.
My question is the following: Why is this government preparing to abandon 1.5 million unemployed Canadians on the battlefield of his made-in-Canada recession, made by this Minister of Finance?
Hear, hear.
Mr. Speaker, I want to remind my hon. friend the last person who used the expression "the mother of all wars" just got wiped out.
Hear, hear.
Possibly my friend will wear his beret into the House tomorrow. He has the moustache.
Hear, hear.
Yes, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance is very fast. Saddam promised the mother of all battles. He delivered the mother of all budgets. And they are both in full retreat.
Hear, hear.
Mr. Speaker, the simple fact of the matter is that this minister-
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member.

Mr. Speaker, the simple fact of the matter is that the government that promised jobs, jobs, jobs is now preparing to leave 1.5 million Canadians unemployed, without shelter, without hope.
Why has the government cut $100 million from job development? Why has this government increased UI premiums by 24 per cent at a time when Canadians are
Oral Questions
being told they are to expect no hope, they are on their own in the face of this recession?
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is wrong again.

We are
reducing the budget of the Canadian Jobs Strategy, that is correct. However, at the same time, we are adding moneys to the amounts that we are putting into training because of the amounts that we are spending in the unemployment insurance fund. We do not like to reduce that amount of funding in the Canadian Jobs Strategy because it is a good program.
Why are you doing it, Michael?

Well, I will tell you why we are doing it. The fact that we are doing this demonstrates the serious nature of the deficit and debt problem.
My hon. friends opposite are being presented with a choice; they can have a healthy economy through lower interest rates or they can have an economy that is going to drag along with high interest rates. The approach of the Liberals and the New Democratic Party as well is to spend, spend, spend, hoping that we are going to get ourselves out of a problem. All it is going to lead to is higher interest rates and a continuation of that problem.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. This budget is a direct attack on the labour movement in this country. The government has effectively declared war on its own employees.
In 1989, more than 68,000 Public Service employees earned less than $30,000 and, interestingly enough, two-thirds of those employees were women.
In light of this, would the Minister of Finance now admit to this House that these measures are aimed solely at the total destruction of the union movement and their rights to bargain in good faith?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Obviously, Mr. Speaker, the government will admit to no such thing. If you have read the budget this year and if you have read the budgets of last year and the year before, you will realize that we are facing a difficult fiscal situation, largely due

Oral Questions
to the very large debt, whether you like it or not, that was left to us by your regime.
To illustrate the dimensions of our problem, in order to service that debt next year we will have to pay in excess of $43 billion. This is a very difficult situation at a time when Canadians are being laid off and losing their jobs, when some are reopening agreements in order to help their companies along. We have had to take difficult measures.
We are not attacking our Public Service, far from it. We are asking them to help us in solving this problem for all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary is for the same minister.
The government's own Labour Canada statistics confirm that the federal employees' wage settlements have fallen far behind both the private sector and the public sector. Based on these figures and those in my previous statement, will the Minister of Finance now agree to abandon these ridiculous plans to control the federal Public Service wages before its own employees take them to task?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the TVeasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have not decided on a wage freeze. We have said there would be a cap on the wage budget.
That being said, I will agree with the hon. member that we have negotiated with the Public Service unions very good agreements. I am proud to say that we have negotiated them below inflation rates. We have managed better than the private sector. We have managed better than other governments and other administrations.
That being said, we are still faced with a fiscal situation. Everybody must bring its share to the solution of that problem. We are taking our cuts and we are bringing in our share. We expect all the employees to participate. I met with all the union leaders this morning except one and we had a very frank exchange. I am very confident that together we can manage this situation.

Mr. Speaker, Canadians needed a budget of hope to get people back to work. What they, got was the same mean ideas which had shut plants, lost jobs and destroyed hope for people right across this country.
My question is directed to the Minister of Finance. In the budget and in Mr. Crow's news conference today, the government committed itself to inflation targets. Will the minister show that he cares about jobs and commit himself to reduce unemployment by setting unemployment reduction targets for this country?

Mr. Speaker, there is a booklet with the budget called Canada's Economic and Fiscal Performance and Prospects. I refer him to page 37 where there is a chart which shows the inflation record of this country in the 1950 to 1973 period and the impact that that had on the economy. Inflation was 2.8 per cent. The deficit, by the way, was at zero.
Federal programs spending was at a low level relative to the size of the economy. Labour productivity was nearly three times what it was in the 1974 to 1984 period, and the growth in the national income was 5.2 per cent in real terms as opposed to 3.3 per cent in real terms in the 1974-1984 period. During that same period the unemployment rate was a good deal lower than it was during the 1974 to 1984 period. That, demonstrates as clearly and as succinctly as I can the benefits of low inflation.

In fact, Mr. Speaker, in the minister's own budget, he projects a 10 per cent unemployment figure and what is worse a 9.8 per cent unemployment figure for next year. Is it not possible for this minister to recognize that there are people hurting across this country, that the anguish that he talked about in his speech is real? Therefore for this minister, it should be just as important to put inflation targets into effect, yes, but just as important to put unemployment targets into effect. Will this minister in fact do that? Will he stand up in the House and commit himself to such targets?

Mr. Speaker, I do recognize that Canadians are hurting. I have heard very directly of the anguish of people losing their jobs and losing their businesses. It is precisely that which drives me to bring in the type of budget we brought in yesterday. It is because this budget is going to bring down interest rates. It is going to bring down inflation. It will result in the employment growth that my hon. friend would like to have.
February 27, 1991

Now, he shakes his head because he does not understand the approach that we are taking. What his-
Oh, oh.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday in his Budget speech the minister justified cuts in spending on the environment as follows: "Since the Green Plan was announced, the economic situation has deteriorated." Mr. Speaker, the Green Plan was announced only two months ago. What does the minister know today that he didn't know two months ago? And what should the minister have known in December that he knows now?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Monday I asked the Minister of Finance about bankruptcies. As we know all too well, Canadians are being hit by bankruptcies in increasing numbers, up by 69 per cent this past January alone.
In the budget speech he gave yesterday we saw a different kind of bankruptcy. It is the political bankruptcy of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance.
When it comes to integrity, this Conservative government is bankrupt. When it comes to fairness, this Conservative government is bankrupt; and when it comes to constructive ideas and compassion, this Conservative government is bankrupt. It is bankrupt when it comes to concern for the needs of ordinary Canadians, workers, fishermen, farmers, small business people, Canadians who live and work along the main streets of this country.

Every Spring for the past seven years, the Minister of Finance has tabled his budget in the House of Commons. Right wing ideologists, who cling to outdated theories, always look forward with impatience to this annual event. Budget number seven will not disappoint them. It contains a great many goodies for them.

For most Canadians there is nothing; nothing positive in this budget. For the majority of Canadians this minister's seven years of budgets have brought only seven years of bad luck.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
His most recent effort does not change Canada's losing streak under this Conservative government. For most Canadians, it is little more
than what has already been called "A Nightmare on Wellington Street, Part VII".
Examples of this nightmare are not hard to find in this budget tabled by the Minister of Finance here in this House yesterday.
In his last budget, the minister put medicare, one of Canada's proudest achievements, on life support; and from this budget the result will likely be that the minister will end up pulling the plug. A full $2.3 billion has been cut from transfers to the provinces for medicare, risking the end of a health care system that has been the envy of the world.
In this budget, the minister has told Canadians that in just a few more years the federal government will be out of the business of supporting medicare. If there is no direct financial involvement in medicare by our federal government, how can we possibly continue to have a national health care system with the same standards from coast to coast to coast.
These cuts in yesterday's budget will also assist in the destruction of post-secondary education. Yesterday, the minister, in effect, told low-income students that their days of education in our post-secondary institutions were numbered.
More than anything else this budget confirms that this Conservative government has placed us all on a path that will lead to the disintegration of Canada. The minister is killing off some of the very programs which have held us together; the programs which have made us proud to be Canadians.
The nightmare does not end there. For the thousands upon thousands of unemployed Canadians this budget offers no hope, but only despair.
Not only does the minister accept that this very high unemployment is here to stay, he is making that high unemployment an integral part of his economic plan. He is telling us without even blinking that this year 10 per cent of Canadians will be unemployed and next year he says it will be more of the same. That is simply obscene, simply obscene.
For the next two years the minister has told us that nearly 1,500,000 Canadians will remain out of work,
1,500,000	people, Mr. Speaker. Instead of doing something about this problem, he simply makes it worse. He
February 27, 1991

gives the unemployed a kick in the teeth not once, but twice. First he slashes $100 million from federal job creation programs. Then he raises unemployment insurance premiums by 25 per cent.
This Minister of Finance, this Prime Minister, this cabinet, and their caucus are pushing hundreds of thousands of Canadians on to the unemployment lines and, even worse, on to the welfare lines.
This budget shows how this government is ducking the blame for its mismanagement, its own mismanagement of the Canadian economy, for when confronted with the grave recession that is causing so much suffering this government blames the economic problems of the United States. It blames the turmoil caused by the war in the Persian Gulf, and when confronted with unemployment the government blames and hurts the unemployed.
When confronted with regional disparity this government blames and hurts our regions. When confronted with thousands of Canadians losing their jobs and thousands of Canadians in desperate need of decent housing, what does the Minister of Finance do? He not only increases unemployment insurance premiums; he actually slashes $411 million from housing programs aimed at helping lower income Canadians.
The facts are clear. The blame lies at the government's own doorstep, and nowhere else. This recession now battering Canadians from coast to coast to coast started well before the Persian Gulf war. It started well before any recession in the United States. It started some 11 months ago, last April in fact. It was initiated by this minister's February 1990 budget and his earlier budgets. If the minister does not want to believe me, he can ask the non-partisan Conference Board of Canada. It told him that last fall his own mismanagement has given us our "first made-in-Canada recession".
The minister should know that already. After all, the recession is the natural result of seven years of narrowminded Conservative policies, particularly their high interest rate policy and their high dollar policy.
And what did the Prime Minister say about all this last October? He confessed, and these are his exact words:
The Budget
We have induced a slowdown. Mr. Wilson said as much in his (last)
budget. Look at the budget-it's as clear as spring water. Mr. Wilson
spelled it out".
That is exactly what the Prime Minister said. If there is one thing that is as clear as spring water, it is that Canadians are mired in a tough unrelenting recession. It is also clear that this government induced the recession. The Prime Minister has said as much.
Something else that is as clear as spring water is that yesterday's budget is going to do nothing, nothing to get us out of that recession. As the economist Michael McCracken of Informetrica said after hearing the budget, and these are his words: "This is a recession making budget". This is what Michael McCracken of Informetrica said and I repeat. He decided this is "a recession making budget".

Mr. Speaker, this government had the gall to decide on our country's economic future on a roll of the dice. All Canadians men and women are the losers. The Minister claimed today, as he did yesterday, that interest rates are coming down. Yet, this reduction is again too little too late. It will take months before this drop in interest rates has any impact.

This is because it will be many, many months before businesses and consumers once again have any kind of real confidence in the economy. But, in the meantime, thousands more Canadians will lose their jobs and thousands more small businesses will go bankrupt.
So what does this budget offer those Canadians and those small businesses? Well, nothing positive, Mr. Speaker, nothing positive at all.
While economic flames rage destroying the lives of Canadians, the minister does nothing constructive, nothing positive and nothing useful. Instead, he fiddles like some modem day Nero and with this budget he is simply stopping his fiddling only to throw more gas on the fire he himself has started.
Economists tell us the recession created by this government could last for many more months, and that is far too long. We Liberals say that what is needed now is more than a new budget. Canadians do not merely want to wait out the recession. They want a new and a better economic plan to lead us out of this recession as soon as possible, and there is no such plan in this budget.

February 27, 1991
The Budget
The Liberals have been calling for a new economic plan since early last summer, one built on much lower interest rates and a much lower dollar. As part of this, Liberals have been calling for adjustment programs to help the firms and the workers hurt, and hurt badly, by the U.S.-Canada free trade deal and by this recession. Liberals have been calling for policies which will help us to restructure, to modernize our work place and retrain our workers. Above all, Liberals have been calling for policies based on fairness. We want to see fair policies which create more jobs, fair policies which bring back strong economic growth, fair policies which end this Conservative government's destruction of our industrial base.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The Prime Minister once promised jobs, jobs and more jobs. Instead, his government has handed Canadians only cuts, cuts and more cuts. It has handed Canadians a good and services tax, a GST that has pushed inflation up to record breaking levels. It has handed them a recession, the Prime Minister has admitted, his government has induced. It has given us high levels of inflation. It has given us an announcement it is seeking free trade with Mexico, without first having any public debate, without first setting out any goals and objectives, and with no effort to undo the damage caused by the Conservative trade deal with the United States.
Yesterday, as the Minister of Finance has done so many times before, he talked about what he plans to do to reduce the deficit, but he does not admit at all that the national debt has doubled, yes doubled, since his government came into power in 1984.
Canadians should not bother to listen to what this Minister of Finance has to say about the deficit and the public debt, because he has no credibility left on this issue or on any other issue.
The minister and the government have their priorities all wrong. The minister is refusing to focus on what is needed, which is to make getting us out of this crippling recession his priority. By failing to do this he is making the deficit problem worse. The minister admits as much on page 70 in his own budget document when he writes:
-the economic situation has deteriorated with a consequent impact on the deficit.
Exactly. What has brought about this deterioration? The Conservative government's own policies, including its support for high interest rates. This has simply made the situation worse. This high interest rate policy has added billions of dollars to the costs of this government's borrowing, and this adds billions to the deficit and to the national debt.
By the way, each time interest rates drop a single percentage point, it saves the government almost $2 billion. If the minister would bother to read his own budget papers, I think he would agree with me, finally. Giving priority to solving Canada's economic crisis will obviously, greatly help the government to deal with its own financial management problems.
The minister's proposed deficit reduction fund, using the proceeds of the GST, is an economic shell game, plain and simple. It adds nothing to government revenues that will not already be there. Meanwhile, the GST itself remains in place to continue to hammer lower and middle income Canadians and create an administrative nightmare for small business.

Mr. Speaker, I urge the Minister of Finance to pause for a moment today to think things over. I urge him to forget the embraces of his Cabinet and caucus friends. I urge him to pause and listen to the voices which can be heard more and more every day outside these walls. I urge the minister and his Cabinet colleagues to listen to the shouts of anger bursting forth everywhere in this country. Canadian men and women have just had enough of this government's callous policies.
More and more Canadians are telling the government that they are fed up with the GST and they will no longer stand any budgetary restraints in the areas of health care and higher education.

Canadians are fed up with the cutbacks to research and development. They are fed up with the way our fishery, agricultural and forestry sectors, the north of our country, and our auto industry have been systematically undermined. They are fed up with the gutting of medicare. They are fed up with cuts to post-secondary education and, as I have already said, they are fed up

with the deterioration of our industrial base, all since this Conservative government came into office.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, Canadians have watched as this government has gutted VIA Rail and shut down post offices all across this country.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Shame.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They watched as this government slashed services and scrapped local television programming by the CBC all across this country.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Shame.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Canadians have watched as this government dismantled the institutions which have helped make this country what it is. They are angry. They want it to stop, but this government does not want to listen to them.
In January and February of this year, while the government was listening to its big business friends on Bay Street, members of the Liberal caucus were crisscrossing the country listening to the real people on Main Street: 35 hearings were conducted by the Liberal caucus, more than 300 submissions were made. We have heard from business associations, labour groups, social action groups, municipalities, provincial government representatives, cultural organizations, and average individual Canadians. The Liberals listened to what Canadians had to say, and what they had to say is this: This Conservative government, this Minister of Finance, this Prime Minister have lost the trust and the confidence of the Canadian people.
The economic policies of this government and this Prime Minister, Canadians have told us, are hurting single mothers, children and small businesses, working men and women and the sick and the elderly. The facts speak for themselves. Economic growth is at the lowest level in 10 years. We have a made-in-Canada Conservative government produced recession, and the most heart-wrenching fact of all: 186,000 Canadian children have been forced to stand in line at food banks across the country; one in six children goes to bed hungry every night.
This budget will not help those hungry children. It will not help working people or small business or farmers or fishermen or anyone else, except maybe the handful of
The Budget
people who still support this government's right wing agenda. But this minister is simply not listening to the overwhelming majority of Canadians.
The words our task force heard were not the words of some narrow corporate elite. They are the words of average Canadians, like the people of my community: auto workers who have seen their jobs disappear forever to the United States and Mexico due to the insensitive policies of this Conservative government. They are the words of Canadians battered by the GST, the free trade agreement and the Conservative government's other insensitive and narrow-minded economic policies.
But does this Minister of Finance, this Prime Minister and this government want to listen? This budget proves they do not. This budget proves that this government is bankrupt when it comes to integrity and constructive ideas. The budget the Minister of Finance has tabled in this House is the last straw. It shows the true face of this government and this cabinet.
They may go around, as the Prime Minister has been doing lately, talking about re-Confederation. But this budget shows us the unvarnished truth, since this budget is simply a blueprint for de-Confederation. The institutions and programs which hold Canada together are being unravelled by this government. Just look at what it has done to VIA Rail, to Canada Post, to the CBC.

And let's take a look at what they are doing to health care and postsecondaiy education. By cutting transfers to the provinces, Mr. Speaker, by the year 2009-which is not that far off-there will be no more federal transfers to the provinces for health care. And if that prediction is correct, the federal government will not be in a position to enforce the standards for health care provided under the Canada Health Act.

There are other examples, but the bottom line is the same. This government is dismantling the institutions and the programs which make Canada great. This government is dismantling the institutions and the programs which define Canada, the institutions which have made us so admired in the eyes of the world. As they move Canada ever closer to the brink of economic and constitutional ruin the minister, the Prime Minister and

February 27, 1991
The Budget
their cabinet colleagues are not listening to what average Canadians have to say any more.
This budget is a Scud missile attack on Canadians. It is an attack on medicare. It is an attack on the jobless. It is an attack on the very institutions and programs that help make up the very fabric that is Canada.
In his budget the minister pays lip service to the notion of a strong and a united Canada.
He cries tears, hopefully not crocodile tears, for Canadian unity. Then, he presents a budget document that is-I repeat-simply a blueprint for de-Confederation.
Yesterday, the minister gave Canadians a blunt lesson in the politics of cruelty. He said to Canadians that they are on their own.
Yesterday, in the midst of a harsh recession the minister told low and middle income Canadians: "You're on your own."
Yesterday, the minister told homeless Canadians that they will just have to make do to get through the winter. He told them that they are on their own.
Yesterday, the minister told sick and elderly Canadians that it does not matter if his policies force provinces to shut down hospitals and lay off doctors and nurses. The minister told sick and elderly Canadians: "You're on your own."
Yesterday, the minister gave us a blueprint for deConfederation and after seeing it, Canadians are saying: "Enough is enough." They are saying: "It is time to stop this Conservative government before it rips this country apart."

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Therefore, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Ottawa South:
That the motion be amended by deleting all of the words after the
word "that" and by substituting the following therefore:
this House condemns the government for presenting a budget that offers no relief to Canadians from the made-in-Canada recession created in 1990, undermines the social and economic foundations of Canadian federalism, increases the already unfair and disproportionate financial burden on lower income and middle income Canadians and provides no program that will, in fact, bring about the recovery of the Canadian economy.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I find the motion in order.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is difficult in responding to a budget not to fall into the trap of choosing rhetoric, phrases and over-statements which make people think that you are not seriously trying to grapple with the way of thinking of the government and the Official Opposition, as opposed to the approaches which we would take in the New Democratic Party, faced with the economic conditions of today.
I want to try to avoid rhetorical flourish. I also want to convey to the House and to the country our sense of profound disappointment in this budget which Mr. Wilson has presented to Canada.
As we listen to people across this country and as our New Democratic economic recovery tour visited different parts of this great country of ours, we heard people say to us just how tough things were, how hard life had become as this recession had begun to bite, how serious and deep the human problems were that they were facing. We heard, for instance, from people such as one of the farmers who talked to us, who talked about what was happening in his community, and I quote directly: "The lay-offs, plant closures, bankruptcies, work sharing, these are only numbers in the paper and at Statistics Canada. But in our community they are real and they hurt". It is a tragic story of broken pride, food bank line-ups, needing welfare assistance, family tensions.
He went on to say that workers between 45 and 64 years of age, many of whom have spent their entire working lives with a single employer, find themselves out in the cold, their jobs eliminated by free trade.
As the director of the Unemployment Help Centre in London said to us: "The social safety net in this country strains under the demands of people hurt by this recession".
As the St. Thomas District Labour Council said to us: "The consequence of a succession of Conservative budgets over the past six years have been devastation for most Canadians". Unemployment is soaring, plant closures and mass lay-offs are everywhere, workers' real average earnings are falling, poverty and hunger are spreading, farm bankruptcies are increasing at a record level and the many victims of these Conservative budgets

are being denied the help they need because of cuts in unemployment insurance and welfare.
Or, as the Waterloo Regional Council said to us: "Seventy per cent of all applicants for welfare in that community are now applying for the first time". Seventy per cent, Mr. Speaker. The total number of recipients of general welfare reached a record high level, higher than they have ever seen before, of over 6,000 in the month of December. In 1989 the Waterloo regional food bank distributed 400,000 pounds of food to people in need. This year they forecast distribution of a million pounds from their food banks to people in need.
As the Community Opportunities Development Association in Cambridge said to us, and they put it very bluntly, if very simply: "The downturn in the economy has put fear into the souls of many members of our community".
That is the reality, Mr. Speaker, which this government seems incapable of recognizing. That is the reality which is devastating lives right across this country, which is destroying families, which is giving people a sense of despair, a sense of pessimism, a sense of fear about the future.
And so I have to say, Mr. Speaker, that I stand up here with a sense of growing fury at this government and its inability to listen to the real voices of people across this country. I say to this government that it is time they recognize the anger, the frustration, the bitterness, the sense of complete and utter failure of hope that hundreds of thousands of Canadians across this country are feeling.
For the sake of this country's future, for the sake of the hundreds of thousands of people being hurt across this country, for the sake of the future of the children of our country, I ask this government to start listening, start to pay attention, start to show you care about those hundreds of thousands of people who are being hurt.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
People wanted a budget of hope and what did they get? They got the same mean message which they have had for the last six and a half years, the
The Budget
same shameful message of cutbacks, of taxes that hit the ordinary person while the large corporations go scot-free; the same fixation on inflation as the concern, the same fixation on the deficit, when it is people across this country who have lost their jobs or have seen their plants shut.
As one person said to me in one of our meetings across the country, "in the 1981-82 recession of the Liberal government, things were bad. We were hurt, but at least we saw the plants were still there. We hoped the jobs would come back and eventually, not because of anything the Liberals did, but because of an upturn in the rest of the world, the jobs did come back and the plants were there for people to go back and work in. The farms were there to give people a sense of prosperity for the future. The small businesses were there."
But this person said to me, "in this recession it is different. In this recession the plants are shutting and they are leaving." They are going to the United States, thanks to free trade. They are going to Mexico and thanks to this government's further foolishness, there will be more of them going to Mexico. More of them will move south. More of them shut and more people hurt across this country as a consequence.
We need a change in direction that says: "Not just targets for inflation, but above all, targets for jobs, for reducing unemployment and for dealing with this recession; targets to get people back to work," so that this country once more starts to work.
It is a very hypocritical budget. It is a budget which talks about the need for national unity. Then in its details cuts back the CBC, destroys national institutions like VIA Rail, and breaks its promises to the provinces.

I am a member from Ontario, but if I were a member from Quebec, if I were a citizen of the province of the Quebec and I were looking at this Budget, I would notice a lot of terms referring to national unity. But what is the real situation? We have a government that has broken its promises to the provinces, that decided that all its promises to the province of Quebec, for instance, were worth nothing, that they could be conveniently ignored or changed or broken!

February 27, 1991
The Budget
The results, for Quebecers and all Canadians, are more unemployment, fewer services, and perhaps the dismantling of our national health care system. We cannot accept that in this country!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We must fight, and I must say that as a party we want to fight this regressive approach. It is not one we can accept, and it would destroy our country.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It's against the interests of Quebec.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is unacceptable.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is one piece of hypocrisy: the discussion of national unity and the lack of any reflection of things that would help to build national unity.
There is also talk of co-operation and how we all must work together. All of us must share the burden. Yet, the reality in the budget is what? It is an attack on workers, on the 6,000 public servants who will lose their jobs.
It is an attack on the possibility of workers being able to keep up with the rate of inflation in the salaries and wages which they receive.
It is an attack on small business.
It is not widely recognized but an increase in unemployment insurance premiums hurts workers. It is true. But, in fact, it hits small business even more than it hits those workers. Small business people across this country will find themselves devastated by the increased burden of these unemployment insurance premiums.
When it comes to workers there are burdens. When it comes to small business there are burdens. When it comes to women there are burdens, as some of the women's groups are cut back as is the support which they have received in the past.
But what about those large companies? What about the big corporations? Is there a single thing in this budget that attacks those corporations? Is there a single thing that asks those corporations to start to pay a fair share? A single thing? Not a single solitary point, not a single change in the tax loopholes that exist, not a single thing to even respond to the willingness which was expressed on the part of some big business groups to
share the burden. Yet, not a single thing was done to make such corporations contribute to the burdens that are falling on workers and on small business people across this country.
There is also discussion in this budget of competitiveness. We all must seek competitiveness.

Competition is important for the future.

We agree. But what is the reality of the budget? The reality is an attack; an attack on education, an attack on science research, an attack on job training, an attack on environmental support. All of those are the basis of future competitiveness in this budget.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yet what does this government do? It cuts. It cuts not for the sake of eliminating waste, because we stood up here in this House and pointed out again and again cases of waste which this government has refused to do anything about.
We had to talk for over two years about grants which were being given to questionable companies in Cape Breton before the government finally recognized that in fact the grants being given were part of a scam and therefore should not be continued.
It took us two years. The member for Nickel Belt and myself fought here in the House, fought in committee. We finally forced the government to recognize the waste which was involved in that particular case. It is so hard to get the government to do something about that sort of waste. It will instead do a few symbolic things like say that it is freezing the salaries of cabinet ministers when, in fact, all that it is freezing is the extra amount which those ministers get as members of the government. They still get their increases as members of Parliament.
We have here an incredible case of hypocrisy within this budget. We have a Minister of Finance who has stood up in the House and said that he heard the anguish of people across this country who had lost jobs and lost their small businesses. He heard that anguish and then he did nothing about it. He did not do a single thing to help people who were being hurt.
February 27, 1991

I would like to move, on behalf of our party, a subamendment to the amendment which has been moved by the Official Opposition. I move:
That the amendment be amended by adding the following words:
"fails to respond to the anguish of people who have lost their jobs or their businesses; undermines the principles of universal medicare; and fails to introduce a program of fair taxation, including a minimum corporate tax."
There was a choice. The government did not take that choice. It kept to the same old path. If it had taken the choice that we put before the country, the many hundreds of thousands hurting across this countiy would be in much better shape.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I will take the subamendment under advisement. I will go to questions and comments. The hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened carefully to the speech by the hon. member for Essex-Windsor, and I must say I was disappointed when he failed to mention the impact of this Budget on federal public servants. If we look at yesterday's Budget speech, on page 10, it says:
The wage budgets of departments will not be adjusted in 1991-92
for any increases in costs arising out of new collective agreements.
Departments will have to absorb any such higher costs from within
existing budgets.
Each increse of 1 per cent in average wage settlements across the
public service could lead to a loss of about 2,000 jobs.

It is quite evident to those of us who care about the Public Service of Canada that the government has declared war on its own public servants. By stating that each per cent increase in wage settlements could lead to
2,000	job losses from the Public Service of Canada, the government is endorsing and promoting the kind of prejudice that some people in this country have against public servants.
This country happens to have one of the best public services in the world. I feel that to not have addressed this question today, which spreads the seed for labour unrest, not only in the Public Service of Canada in the years to come, but in other departments. For the NDP,
The Budget
who are the socialists of this countiy, what I like to call the arm-chair socialists, not to have alluded in one sentence in the speech to the labour unrest we are going to be suffering because of this government's lack of sensitivity is beyond my understanding.
I want to ask the member from Essex-Windsor, why is it that his party and his opening speech on this most important budget speech did not once mention the impact of this budget on labour in general? Specifically, why did he not address the impact on the Public Service of Canada, the public servants of this country who are doing a damned good job for Canada?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, every time a spokesperson from the Liberal Party gets up to defend workers, I have to say that I am especially amused. I am especially amused when they get up to defend public servants, because this member and his party, if the hon. member would remember back a few years, was the very party that brought into effect controls on public servants-the six and five program which was opposed bitterly by the Public Service across this country and across the community of Ottawa. Let me tell you that the impact on morale in the Public Service, which is certainly going to be very negative over what the Conservatives have done in this budget, was also extremely negative over what the Liberals did during the 1981-1982 recession when they did precisely the same thing. They tried to make workers into the cause of that recession instead of recognizing that in fact working people are very much those who are hurt by recession.
If the member had listened to my speech he would also have noticed that I did in fact talk precisely about the
6,000	jobs that this Conservative approach to the Public Service will likely lead to being lost. Those 6,000 jobs will be lost if public servants take their full 3 per cent increase, which itself is well below the rate of inflation. That will force an elimination of jobs within the Public Service.
Now if the member did not recognize that I was talking about the sections of the budget which deal with the Public Service in noting those 6,000 potential job losses then it shows that despite his past work he really does not understand very well the way in which these particular measures from the Conservative Party are going to

February 27, 1991
The Budget
negatively impact public servants here in Ottawa and across the country.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the member for Windsor-Essex mentioned the small business community and how it was going to be hurt. I would like to describe, in my introductory remarks here, how the unemployment insurance filters down and, as employers, how this is going to affect the small business community. Not only directly, but in the municipalities. These increases in unemployment insurance, the increases in Established Programs Financing or the cuts to Established Programs Financing and the cap on the Canada Assistance Plans all filter through to the provinces and through to the municipalities.
The biggest employers in most small communities across Canada are municipalities, hospitals and school districts. These people and these groups are going to be hurt directly by UI and by the cuts in these various programs. Those people are going to have to pick the money up somewhere and pass it down to the taxpayers through property taxes and through provincial taxes. In this way it also hurts.
My question to the member is this. Would he agree that, although the government has told us there will not be tax increases, in fact, once again, the low and middle income earners are being hit by tax increases by underhanded methods of this government?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the member has made a veiy important point. I want to just indicate to the House some of the comments which we received from small business people during our economic recovery tour in different parts of the country.
For instance, as somebody said to me in my own community in the hearings that we held there: "The GST, the high dollar and the recession are killing us". This person is the head of the Downtown Business Persons Association in my community. We have to recognize what this government is doing this year. It is, first, putting a very serious burden on small business with the introduction of the GST. The level of administrative cost that small business will have to absorb is extremely heavy. Many small business people across the country have talked to me about the damage that is going to be
done to their prospects for the future as a result of that administrative cost.
In addition to that GST impact, the government has now decided as well to increase unemployment insurance premiums. And, as I indicated in my speech, that is going to impact most on small businesses across this country because, of course, small businesses pay $1.4 for every $1 that a worker pays into the unemployment insurance fund. That is just one example of the way in which the unfairness that this government has put into effect in past budgets continues in this budget, and it is one of the reasons why we oppose this budget so strongly.
