speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Blais (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Minister of State (Agriculture)):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Minister of State (Agriculture)
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to lead off the debate on the Budget on behalf of the government side in this House. After listening to my NDP colleagues who are up there in the clouds, I think we should get down to earth, for a change.
I must say I was puzzled when the hon. member for Windsor West said we had to create jobs for Canadians but certainly not open our markets to the United States and even less to Mexico. Far too dangerous! Let's create jobs here to produce goods. And where would we sell them? That, of course, is a minor problem. It is a minor problem for NDP members who don't have a clue about government finances and financial administration, about being competitive and being able to manufacture goods and sell them at competitive prices. It doesn't fit their vision and concept of society.
However, after the Minister of Finance brought down his Budget yesterday, others did react, Mr. Speaker. Frederic Wagniere, in this morning's La Presse, qualified this Budget as honest and far-sighted. He said it had been a long time since we had a budget that reconciled both the government's financial requirements and the economic interests of Canadians. He went on to say that the government had understood the gravity of Canada's economic and financial situation and had decided to do something about it. Mr. Speaker, Mr. Wagniere also said

that the Budget was straight forward in that it meets problems head on, without compromising our economic future in the long term.
Mr. Speaker, clearly these people are far more objective than the hon. member for Essex-Windsor, as far as I could gather from his comments. I believe that the plan for economic recovery set forth in the Budget brought down yesterday puts Canada and Canadians on the path to renewed and sustained prosperity. The key to dynamic economic recovery and the nation's future growth and prosperity is obvious.
Interest rates must go down and remain at low levels for some time. To achieve this, we will have to meet a very basic requirement, equally obvious, which is to bring about a continuing and sustained reduction in inflation and the inflationary expectations of Canadians. Incidentally, Mr. Speaker, I heard another member from the Windsor area say that an unemployment rate of 10 per cent was obscene. I find such comments hard to accept, coming from the Liberals, since at the time they inflicted unemployment rates on Canadians that in some parts of the country were as high as 20 per cent, and interest rates that for a while were as high as 24 per cent, with 12 per cent inflation- there was for instance- Perhaps the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There will be opportunity for questions and comments a little later.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Minister of State (Agriculture)
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can assure you that Canadians who had to fork over these huge amounts and pay the astronomical cost of that recession are not about to forget it. Indeed this is why they saw fit at the time to get rid of those great administrators, those glorified public clerks, and replace them by a government which proved to be responsible during its first mandate from 1984 to 1988 and which will continue to steer the country towards prosperity with the measures unveiled yesterday.
Mr. Speaker, of course there is a direct link between inflation and interest rates, as evidenced by our past economic performance. During the 1950s and 1960s when inflation was low-averaging less than 3 per cent a
The Budget
year-interest rates were low as well. When inflation rose in the 1970s, so did interest rates.
Comparisons with other countries confirm the existence of that link. Between 1980 and 1989 the major industrialized countries of the Group of Seven where inflation was lowest on average-Japan and Germany- were also those where average interest rates were lowest too. Then there were countries where inflation was left running rampant. For example, France and Italy generally recorded the highest interest rates, and that was unfortunate for those people. Mr. Speaker, we are working to bring about such conditions as will enable the economy to get back on an even keel by the middle of this year, not in five years, this year. And we are making progress because interest rates have already declined by more than four points since last May's peak. Canadian consumers throughout the country will see for themselves when they renew their mortgages or personal loans in the coming weeks that indeed they have more money in their wallets to cope with present conditions precisely because their interest rates will have gone down by 2, 3 and 4 per cent.
Still if we hope for a sustainable economic growth we cannot be satisfied with getting a handle on inflation. Our national objective must be to check inflation and then reduce it considerably and keep it down. Price stability spells enormous economic and social benefits, and lower interest rates are just one of a good many others.

Price stability is vital for Canadian companies and workers to compete and succeed in today's global marketplace.
With inflation, Canadian products can end up costing more than comparable goods sold by other countries. This means companies lose sales and workers lose jobs.
Price stability also supports increased investment by business.
Research indicates that lower inflation is one reason the cost of investment capital is lower in Japan and Germany than in Canada and the United States. Economic fairness is another crucial reason why Canadians should work toward lower inflation. Keeping price increases down is simply the best way to protect those with the least ability to protect themselves against inflation:

February 27, 1991
The Budget
the poor, the elderly, and people on fixed incomes. These are compelling reasons why our plan for economic recovery takes direct aim at reducing inflation further.
The budget announced realistic achievable inflation targets. They are based on the Consumer Price Index, the most commonly used measure of inflation. The official targets are: by the end of 1992, an inflation rate of 3 per cent; by mid-year 1994, inflation down to 2.5 per cent; and the year after, by the end of 1995, an inflation rate of 2 per cent. I think that this is achievable.
Clearly, in the words of Terence Corcoran in The Globe and Mail this morning:
- Mr. Wilson has defied many forecasters with a deficitcontrolling, opposition-rattling Recovery Budget.
[Translation\
After 1995, as I explained, Mr. Speaker, the government will continue its efforts to achieve price stability. The goals and methods then adopted will be based on the experience gained over the next few years and on the continuing consultations of Canadians. The inflation targets described in the government's Plan for Economic Recovery make sense and, in my opinion, are necessary. Canada had much lower inflation rates in the past and is able to equal this performance. It is only since the 1970's that Canada's performance has deteriorated compared to those of such countries as Germany and Japan.
There is no reason why Canada could not repeat its performance of those years, provided we work together to reach this goal.
The benefits of a lower inflation rate are evident and concrete. Interest rates would be coming down, as they are currently doing, Mr. Speaker. Our economic productivity and competitiveness would be strenghtened. Already second in the world, our standard of living would improve, and so would our social equality. Consequently, Canada would be a stronger and more prosperous country which could rank among the economic leaders, Mr. Speaker.
With this budget, we are putting government finances firmly on the course to a balanced budget. We are taking steps to eliminate the build-up of the public debt as a source of inflationary concern. For this purpose, we are extending by nearly three years until 1994-95 the Expenditure Control Plan developed in the 1990 budget. Of course, this decision does not please our NDP friends whose only policy is to spend more and more, because they think that throwing away borrowed money can help a country prosper. Clearly their position does not have the support of any economists, except their own, and as everybody knows, Mr. Speaker, has no credibility among Canadians.
We are legislating mandatory program spending limits and we are setting up a Debt Servicing and Reduction Fund solely dedicated to offsetting the costs of the public debt. By law, all revenues from the Goods and Services Tax and from privatization will flow into this fund. This way, Mr. Speaker, we expect to achieve our goal in time-it will not be easy and will require time, energy and determination-but I am convinced that we can do it.
Also, the government and its civil servants will do their share. We will severely restrain the operations of the government. Operating budgets will be frozen at current levels and the wages and salaries of Cabinet Ministers will be tightly restrained. Severe restrictions will be placed on the salaries paid to members of Parliament and senators as well as all federal civil servants and any person designated by an Order in Council from this government. That is why it was said, Mr. Speaker, and I am again quoting from this morning's edition of Le Soleil: "Wilson sets the example."
I think that it would be extremely difficult for the government to ask the Canadian people to make sacrifices, while allowing its own expenditures to keep growing by 8,10 or 12 percent. Of course, we could very easily go on spending. There is nothing easier, Mr. Speaker. We could borrow and establish programs, as our predecessors did for years. That is how they created a structural deficit which had reached $200 billion when we came to power. It is so easy. Any government can borrow money, establish programs and spend irresponsibly.

speechtext: And foot the bill later!

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Minister of State (Agriculture)
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if we want our children and grandchildren to enjoy prosperity in this country, we have no choice but to make government accountable. We appreciate that these measures are very hard on the

government. They are hard on our employees. They are indeed, but we have no choice.
In a family faced with a shrinking income for one reason or another, the father and mother sit around the kitchen table and decide on ways to reduce overall expenditures so that money will be assigned to specific purposes and earmarked for the neediest. That is how we came to earmark more than $7 billion in spite of the difficult economic context. We managed to identify an amount totalling over $7 billion which is earmarked for the unemployed who are the neediest this year. We understand what they are going through. There is also $1.6 billion for the elderly and another $1.3 billion for farm producers who are struggling for reasons beyond our control and having to do with the global environment.
I think it is wise to consider and respond to the needs of particular groups, Mr. Speaker.
The programs I mentioned earlier account for over 90 percent of the financial support given by the federal government to the provinces in order to help them finance a wide range of important services across Canada. That is essential. No wonder that the Budget that was tabled yesterday has some major effects on the federal-provincial fiscal arrangements, particularly on some components of the transfer payments system to the provinces, that is, the Equalization program, the Established Programs Financing and the Canada Assistance Plan.

For decades, the federal government has provided large and growing financial support to the provinces. Next year alone, total federal transfers, including both cash and tax transfers, will reach almost $37 billion.
The cash portion alone of the transfers accounts for one-fifth of all federal program spending. These transfers are simply too large to exempt from our expenditure restraint program.
The deficit is a national problem and it demands a national solution. Major transfers to the provinces, both cash and tax, will grow by an average of 3.7 per cent per year from 1991-92 to 1995-96. All other federal program spending will grow by just 3.4 per cent. It should be noted that the 1991 budget has no effect on transfers in the current fiscal year or the next.
The Budget
For 1990-1991 and 1991-1992 transfers will be made on the basis of the February 1990 budget, which provinces have already factored into their planning. The new measures in this year's budget will cause 1992-1993 transfer growth to be reduced by roughly $700 million or about one-half of one per cent of provincial revenues.
In addition, the measures are tailored so as to have a smaller impact on the low income provinces.

I think, Mr. Speaker, that we have taken the necessary measures to insure that our initiatives with regard to the provinces are just and fair. I think that ultimately, as the Minister of Finance of Newfoundland said last night, the Minister of Finance's approach is just and fair and, despite certain difficulties that we appreciate, we will be able to cope with the situation.
The cap on the growth of transfer payments for Established Programs Financing raises concerns about the ability of the federal government to continue enforcing national medicare principles under the Canada Health Act.
Legislation will be introduced to ensure that the federal government continues to have the means to enforce these principles. As we said yesterday, and as we are saying again today, the principles of the Canadian Health Act will not be compromised.
The measures in this budget bring the growth of transfer payments to the provinces into line with current fiscal realities. But it is also time to ask ourselves whether the system of tranfers and tax arrangements can be reformed to better meet the energing challenges, priorities and needs of the 90s and beyond.
The federal government will consider reforms to the major transfer programs within the fiscal framework set out in this budget. In this regard, we will keep in mind that one of the best things we can do to strengthen national unity is improving our economy and our financial position. We want to ensure that, in the future, the system of transfers provides for the sharing of opportunities and benefits of Confederation, supports a more efficient and competitive Canada, and maintains the principles and standards that are the basis of Canadian citizenship while respecting provincial flexibility.

February 27, 1991

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last night as I listened to the Minister of Finance deliver his seventh budget, I asked myself: "Where are the ideas that could animate and inspire a whole generation?" Ideas, visions and principles move a nation, and for ideas to have meaning they must be returned to their centre. That centre is the human being; the human being suffering, working, striving and hoping. This is where I think the Minister of Finance and his advisers have failed. They have failed to relate to the human being. Our distinct Canadian society is centred in the person.
This minister talked about a national exercise to bring together the ideas and efforts of all Canadians. But for an effective and meaningful national exercise, trust must be the first rung on the ladder. For a minister of finance to earn trust, people will look at his track record, past and present. Does the past track record of the Minister of Finance build the trust factor or diminish it?
I would suggest over seven budgets of cuts, cuts, cuts-and I do not talk about cuts to eliminate waste, I talk of cuts because of lack of creativity. There have been multiple tax increases on the personal side, GST, sell-offs, giveaways of Terminal Three; a litany of forecasts never achieved. The trust factor on being sincere about reducing the deficit from 1984 to 1988 when we had one of the best economic performances in this country, where was the effort to reduce or hold the deficit and the debt then? He supervised. He was the Minister of Finance when the deficit went from $180 billion to $370 billion and blamed all of that on Liberals who were not in

The Budget
power. The trust factor for this minister is on precarious ground.
Let us talk about the present, last night's budget. Once again, the cornerstone of this government's plan, its Speech from the Throne, was the environment. And right off the bat we see in last night's budget cuts again. The Canada Assistance Plan which will affect our municipalities; Telefilm Canada cuts; Science and Technology, which affects our research and development, which affects our training, something we need so badly to meet the competitive levels that the Minister of Finance talks about.
Elousing. We have the worst state in our history for affordable shelter in this country, and what does the Minister of Finance do instead of trying to alleviate this problem? He pulls back over five years $411 million.
I am going to mention the Toronto Ballet Opera House. I am going to mention it because on the face of it, it would seem that the minister does not realize that a ballet house is not just for those who go to the ballet. The ballet is a cultural contribution and this is one of the greatest industries that we have in this country. It is also for tourism which is the biggest job creator in this country. But, once again, he has misread it and it is cut.
The same with cultural centres in other parts of the country.
Wage controls for the Public Service. The Minister of Finance does not realize that now with the problems we are having during a recession, with the unemployment rates going so high, with the problems we are having in immigration because of refugee backlog, with the problems we are having at Canada Mortgage and Housing, that at this time more than ever we need our Public Service to really give the kind of service that supports all of us as parliamentarians. So, when you sort of come along and spit in their faces, as we have done with this budget, that affects morale, that affects productivity and that affects the mood of this entire country.
When it comes to the present and we look at this budget, once again I see that the Minister of Finance's trust factor is again diminished.
The minister used the words "national exercise", "national unity", "faith", "Canadian value system". We have the world's second highest standard of living.
I am absolutely amazed when I hear this group of Conservatives rediscovering the word "national".
I am amazed because for the last six years they have been decentralizing and denationalizing and retreating from national programs and national standards as if they were in some form of a dismantling race.
When I hear the Minister of Finance use the word "national", I feel it is like some kind of a deathbed conversion.
I want to repeat that the human being is where we must begin.
I suggest that human beings want to be treated fairly. When fairness is a part of the national mood, then productivity will increase. Then, and only then, will the objectives of lower interest rates, lower inflation, lower cost of goods, full employment happen. Only when a human being feels like he is being treated fairly can the trust factor take hold.
I believe that the instrument the Minister of Finance has to begin that national mobilization that he talks about, to begin that galvanization, the instrument that he has at his disposal is the tax system. It is the one instrument that touches everyone coast to coast and the Minister of Finance ignored that instrument. He ignored it last night. He had one page in this budget devoted to the tax system and said: "Over the next few months we will listen to people. We will listen to their ideas and then we will go from there".
How can trust be present unless we begin with the human being and that is where the Minister has failed. He is looking at a set of numbers in a macro sense, but he is not going back to basics.
The way we galvanize the will of this nation is by treating people fairly. We know that the current tax system in this government, run by this government right now, and I will say that previous governments which we were a part of, is in sad shape and needs a major overhaul. The Minister of Finance failed to have the courage to address it in last night's budget.
I want to mention Mr. Yves Seguin, who was Minister of Revenue for Quebec until six months ago when he resigned over the GST. He said last night on Radio-Ca-

nada, the French CBC network, Le Point: "Canadian unity is in danger if the tax system is not profoundly reformed. It is favouring the rich more than ever".
How can trust be present with a minister who has failed to address the human being? What we have here as a result of that is a policy document with no moral substance. Therefore, I say, that with every good intention of this minister, this document is going to end up like the previous six where very little of it will come to reality.

Mr. Speaker, I listen to the speeches of members of the opposition and I am having some difficulty with examples they give.
I will first make a comment then ask a question, Mr Speaker. We know the budget is divided roughly into three parts: one third for the servicing of the debt, about one third for transfers to the provinces and the other third for programs. When we came into office in 1984, debt servicing cost about $200 billion and we had to borrow approximately $30 billion a year just to pay interests on that debt.
If my arithmetic is right, $30 billion multiplied by seven years amount to $210 billion, plus the $200 billion we inherited in 1984, $410 billion all told. This is about what figures now reveal.
I listen carefully when the members of the opposition tell us that we do not cut down on the right expenses. Well, it is impossible to reduce the service of the debt that calls for the third of the budget. As for the transfers to the provinces, the minister said earlier that he did not reduce them in the budget. So, that leaves the federal programs to be examined.
I would like to ask a question to the Hon. Member who has just made such an eloquent speech. If we examine the federal programs-as the minister himself suggested it-how could we rearrange the system so to recover adequate amounts of money first to pay the debt and second to improve the lot of Canadians?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to respond to the hon. member by saying that first of all when his party took power, the debt was approximately $180 billion and the interest payments during that first year were closer to $18 billion because of the current rate of tax and other
The Budget
accesses his party had to foreign capital. So when he uses numbers like $30 billion and $200 billion I do not mind a small increase, but when he is almost doubling, I get a little disturbed.
The point of the matter is, his party took power when we had one of the best economic performances ever. The Minister of Finance last night talked about setting up this reserve fund, this debt reduction fund, which I think is an interesting idea. My point would be that he mentioned when he was the finance critic in opposition in 1982 and 1983 that he was going to come in and attack this deficit, this debt problem. Why did he not implement some of those ideas at that time when he had an economy that was working in his favour? That was the time to begin acting on his words.
When we have a severe recession on our hands, it is not the time to ignore those 1.5 million people who are unemployed.
If these 1.5 million people are put to work, it will generate revenue and that will pay down the debt and the deficit a heck of a lot faster than an almost programmed unemployment. With 1.5 million people unemployed the entire social safety net becomes stressed to the point where we are locked into these deficit and debt numbers. That is where we take exception.
We hear about job creation programs being gutted and tourism programs being gutted and the small business of this nation, which employs 80 per cent of the labour, being threatened by an almost 150 per cent increase in UI premiums. That is not how to get an economy working again. That further demoralizes it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I congratulate my colleague from Broadview-Greenwood for an excellent presentation.
When he talks about putting people at the centre of things that we do, I think he is on the right track.
I want to remind my colleague from Toronto about a debate we had two and a half years ago about the free trade agreement. Our concern at that time was something that we called harmonization, in particular harmonization with certain social programs in the United States. Our concern was that this Conservative government would drag down our social programs to the level of the Americans, in other words, reducing our social programs to the lowest common denominator.
And what have we seen? I will give two examples. In the budget of yesterday there was an increase of 24 per cent in UIC premiums. UIC has been disavowed in this country. The government has backed off from unemployment insurance, a la the American style.
What about medicare? The same dismal story. The government is backing away from medicare. More than $2 billion was taken out of transfer payments in this budget alone.
In my opinion what we have is harmonization; harmonization that is rampant. I would like to know from my colleague from Toronto whether he sees exactly the same thing.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity today to speak in support of the budget that was presented by the Minister of Finance last night.
This budget is consistent and can be taken in the context of the long list of economic reforms and restructuring that we have been pursuing over the past six years. At that time we set out on economic and non-economic fronts to deal with, what were in some cases, long outstanding problems that were the country and restricting us from reaching our true potential.
During that time we reformed the energy sector through abolition of the National Energy Program and deregulation. We reformed the transportation sector through deregulation. We reformed the investment sector through abolition of the Foreign Investment Review Agency to allow for increased foreign investment, especially needed in resource areas of the country like Alberta and western Canada.
We have been privatizing Crown corporations. We are trying to expand trade opportunities through such measures as the Free Trade Agreement with the United States and are now examining the possibility of a trilateral trade agreement between Canada, the United States, and Mexico.
We made major reforms to the unemployment insurance program. The list goes on and on.
All of these have been an attempt to make the Canadian economy more market oriented, more able to compete in international markets. I believe each of these steps has been positive in itself. Frankly, on most of them we have no choice.
The world economy has undergone and is continuing to undergo radical change. If we think back to 20 or 30 years ago, there were a few industrialized countries like our own producing most of the industrial products and services for the rest of the world. We think of countries like Japan back in the fifties and sixties. They were thought of as producing low quality products that nobody really wanted. We do not think of Japan in that way any more. The same can be said for countries such as Taiwan, Korea, now Thailand, and others, which have gradually moved to value added high technology products that now compete with the best that we can produce here in Canada.
The Budget
We are currently seeing a virtual revolution going on in eastern Europe. Those countries have recognized that they must move forward and they must become more market oriented if they are going to share in the same kind of economic benefits as has the rest of the world.
What this means is that we no longer have a monopoly on technology and industrial production that we used to share with a few other countries. Today, our former customers are now our competitors. But we have always been and continue to be a trading nation, the second most dependent nation in the world on trade.
Now trade, investment and capital flows are more international than ever before. It is competition that we have not known in the past or at least not known to this degree, and it is probably going to be much more severe in the future. This means that we have to prepare ourselves for what is coming.
I believe that these structural reforms, along with the signals that have been given in yesterday's budget, put us in a position to do that. On page 51 of the budget document reference is made to this:
The government's structural reforms, implemented since 1984, have helped raise the economy's potential growth rate from about 2 3/4 per cent during the 1980s expansion to a projected 3 1/4 per cent over the medium term.
That increased capacity of approximately three-quarters of a percentage point of real growth per year is where we can find the resources, among other things, to deal with the deficit and debt problem we are concerned about, but also on an ongoing basis free up money and capacity to do the kinds of things that most of would like to get on with.
The potential growth rate is determined by the growth of labour, capital and total productivity. As noted on page 51:
The Free Hade Agreement with the United States, deregulation of industries, and the effect of the GST will stimulate capital spending. The capital stock is expected to grow 4.4 per cent a year over the medium term, up from 3.5 per cent-The structural reforms will also raise total factor productivity growth which should average 0.5 per cent a year compared with virtually no growth during (the last) expansion.
While aggregate output growth is expected to be similar over the 1993-96 period to that recorded between 1984-87, there will be many differences in the over-all performance of the economy. Much more of the growth will come from business fixed investment and a net trade balance than in the previous expansion which was led by

The Budget
growth and consumption, both by households and governments.
Productivity performance should also be better. These differences in the composition of growth, more supply and less consumption will contribute to fundamentally lowering inflation pressures and an improved competitive position internationally. The economy will therefore be in a much better position in 1996 than it was toward the end of the 1980s.
By 1996, Canadians, under this scenario can achieve an economy with no government sector debt, no current account deficit, no net reliance on foreign savings, and low inflation. This represents a return of the more balanced economic type of environment that we had been 1950 and the mid-1970s.
In short, we will have set for sustained growth and prosperity rather than the wrenching cycles that we have been going through between the 1970 and 1980 period.
How do we achieve this? I guess what is important in the message from the Minister of Finance's budget last night is the fact that fundamentally we must continue to keep the growth in the deficit and debt under control. The only way to manage and keep sustained growth in the economy is to keep interest rates low on a permanent basis. High public sector deficits do not allow for that.
Many people do not understand the relationship between government debt and interest rates. Essentially, there is only so much money available in an economy from the savings that people have put into retirement plans and other savings instruments. If the government consumes all those savings or a substantial part of them, it crowds out demand from other sources such as business which wants to borrow for investment. Essentially the price then goes up or interest rates go higher, meaning our companies and Canadian business cannot compete in the capital markets against other countries where capital is available at a lower rate. We have seen this, for example, in Germany and Japan.
There is no other way of doing this. Other countries have tried. They have tried, for example, printing money, which is about the only other choice. That just simply does not work.
Sometimes in this House we tend to talk as if the government and the Bank of Canada can set interest rates simply where they wish, with no other consequences. The fact of the matter is their ability to do that is limited. Essentially, international capital markets are going to have a much more greater influence in the things we do in Canada.
That is why, in order to establish the environment for lower interest rates, we must give the signal that both public sector debt as well as inflation are going to be maintained under control. That is why in his budget last night the Minister of Finance dwelt essentially on those two items, because both are related.
If we keep inflation under control or reduce it to the 2 per cent level that he is seeking, this sets the environment for lower interest rates on an ongoing, sustained and permanent basis. This naturally reduces the cost of borrowing for everyone, including the government, which means that the debt we carry will be easier to pay the interest on. As well, we will be able to start to reduce that debt because after about the middle of this decade, about 1995, we will hopefully be in a position where we will not be issuing any more new government bonds.
Of course all of these are predicated on some assumptions, but I believe that the Minister of Finance in his budget last night has made realistic assumptions, as realistic as anyone can make given the nature and times that we are living in. None of us, for example, a year ago in the budget debate would have expected to have gone through a war between then and now. We will likely face other challenges between now and next year's budget.
I think what the Minister of Finance has shown last night is that he is prepared to make the adjustments necessary to stay on track. He set the track several years ago. He has consistently addressed this every year. Adjustments are required and he made them. We have made some adjustments again in terms of the public sector and what we plan to do as a government. We have done that, to send a signal to the private sector so that it can have the confidence that the economic climate, inflation and interest rates will be maintained and that levels of inflation and interest rates will be reduced.

Hopefully this will bring the kind of investment stimulus that we are all looking for and the kind of job creation that we would all like to see.
I would like to say one thing, because I see there is a member of the Liberal Party seeking to ask me a question.
I enjoyed his speech, by the way. He talked about tax reform, which is a favourite topic of his recently. I wonder if he could comment, while he is asking his question, on when he is prepared to come to the finance committee and explain his proposal, because we had to postpone the meeting which was scheduled before Christmas.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all, I will address the question regarding the single tax, which is a fairer and simpler system than the one we have on the table now. It needs refinement and modifications, which I am doing in conjunction with my leader's tax task force.
Our single tax team would be happy to appear before the finance committee in the not too distant future. We hope that we will provide some creativity for him.
My question has to do with the dollar. I notice that the Minister of Finance last night never talked about the dollar, and none of the speakers today on the government side talked about the dollar. We all want to increase our competitiveness, we all want to get full employment going again, and we are all concerned about exports.
I would like to know the member's thoughts on bandying the dollar around 78 and 82 cents. He never mentioned his thoughts on the dollar during his speech. I wonder if he would elaborate on what he thinks that might do to stimulate exports, which would take people off the unemployment rolls. That in itself would not have a great effect on inflation or interest rates in my opinion, but at the same time would probably take less drag on the deficit.
What are his thoughts on that?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I would like to say that when he gets his caucus to agree to his tax proposal, I can assure him that I will have no problem in getting mine to support it.

speechtext: Did you hear that?

speechtext: Absolutely.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
As far as the question about the dollar, there is often debate as to whether or not the dollar is too high relative to the productivity in the country. But when he suggests that somehow we can bring this dollar down, one has to ask: how does this happen?
There is a suggestion that the Bank of Canada has been doing something to keep the dollar high. In fact, the numbers do not bear that out. Foreign reserves are at an all-time high, something in excess of $20 billion. What that means is that the Bank of Canada has been intervening in financial markets, essentially to try and keep the dollar from going even higher.
Beyond intervening in those markets and accumulating even higher degrees of foreign reserves, there really is not any direct way of dealing with it unless we are prepared to impose some kind of currency controls.
We used to have a fixed dollar; we used to have it fixed to the United States. But that was abandoned because, essentially, it did not work. The government could not make it stick. There was simply too much pressure on the dollar. There were too many dollars available for sale that the government then had to buy up, and that policy was abandoned. Most countries in the world that have had those kinds of policies have also abandoned them.
There is really no industrial country in the world at the moment, that I can think of, that has this kind of policy. The Europeans are trying to bring about a more common currency. The Deutschmark does dominate the economy there-and they do intervene-but in part that is because they have the Bundesbank in Germany essentially supporting that. For us to peg the dollar to the United States dollar would, for the most part, require us to get the Americans to agree to assist us. I am not sure that they would, in the first place, and probably we would not want them to do that.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened carefully to the member's address. If I understood it correctly, the member has great faith in the prognostications and tea-leaf reading ability of the Minister of Finance. I of course do not have that same faith.
I would like to ask three specific questions to the member, addressed to some of the prognostications that

February 27, 1991
The Budget
were made by the finance minister last year as compared to what he in fact said last night in his budget speech.
He said last night, and I quote, "We will hold the deficit to $30.5 billion this year and next"-I repeat, $30.5 billion this year and next-"despite the pressures of recession". Then he predicts that the deficit will fall next year below $25 billion for the first time in a decade. I ask the hon. member, does he believe that, in view of the fact that last year the Minister of Finance did not say that he was going to hold the deficit, but rather predicted that it was going to be below $30 billion? He did not predict a recession, which he himself made.
Later in his speech he said, and I quote: "The economic recovery will begin in the second half of this year and accelerate next year". So the question is: Does the member believe that statement, in view of the fact that last year the finance minister in no way in his speech predicted that this year there would be a recession? On the contrary, he predicted the exact opposite and was wrong.
Finally, he predicted in his speech yesterday-he was talking about interest rates-that the interest rates will be well below the 1990 average of 13 per cent. Indeed, the 1990 average was 13 per cent, but I am sure the member will remember that the finance minister predicted that they would not be anywhere near 13 per cent when he delivered his budget in 1990.
I ask the member: Does he believe in the prognostications of the Minister of Finance on those three points, three points on which he was 100 per cent dead wrong one year ago? If he does, why has the minister's future seeing ability, clairvoyance, suddenly got better?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will try to respond to that as briefly as I can because I think we are nearly out of time.
First of all, yes, I do believe that the minister will meet his targets. I think that anyone involved in predicting economics, or for that matter in budgeting in a business, would recognize that in terms of the order of magnitude we are talking about a difference in the deficit between what was predicted and what it is now coming in at of about $1 billion to $2 billion.
In government we use billions, but in business we deal with either thousands or millions. In order of magnitude
with a $150 billion approximate expenditure budget, we are talking about something between a 1 and 2 per cent variance here. I think that with any business plan that comes in with a 1 or 2 per cent variance, most businessmen would think they had been pretty close.
In terms of the economic recovery, the member has asked why do I believe that that will start in mid-year. I think that is probably a good case because last year it was expected that the economic slowdown would come sooner than it did. In fact, it came somewhat later in the year, which probably means that the recovery now projected is going to begin somewhat sooner than we might have thought last year.
As far as interest rates, the fact that the economy remains stronger than predicted for a period of time is one of the reasons interest rates also remain higher. What we are seeing now is the response. Interest rates have fallen; the demand for borrowing and credit has been reduced. In all likelihood, I think if anything the Minister of Finance's projections are probably conservative.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a number of my colleagues have already or will shortly speak on specific aspects of the budget and how they affect Canadians in various regions of our country and in various sectors of our economy, the adverse impact that the budget will have on the expectations of Canadians during this period of recession.
I want to spend a few moments in this budget debate on the question of where the government has come from and pick up a point that my colleague from Scarborough just touched upon, and that is the credibility of the government and of the Minister of Finance in offering Canadians their budget forecast for the time ahead.
The Minister of Finance and the government enjoy nothing more than to attempt to blame the current recession on the Liberal government in the period prior to 1984. This seems like a footling waste of time of the House of Commons and indeed of the people of Canada to engage in such surrealistic thinking. The fact remains that, in statistical terms, what the government says when it attempts to blame a previous government for its present dilemmas is nonsense.

I shall offer the House one example and then proceed to a consideration of the background of the budget itself.
The Minister of Finance enjoys, it seems, pointing to the 1980-81 recession when interest rates were over 20 per cent. But what he does not add is that at that same time inflation was 12.5 per cent. Not only in Canada, but globally inflation was high. In Canada it was 12.5 per cent, so that the real interest rates were 7.5 per cent.
What happened in May 1990 when this government and this Minister of Finance were in office? Interest rates were at 14.1 per cent, inflation was 4.4 per cent. So the real interest rates in May 1990 were 9.7 per cent and in 1981, as I say, they were only 7.5 per cent, so who is fooling whom? The fact is that this government has made its own recession. It has created its own recession. At a time when interest rates could have been much lower, the government pursued its wrong-minded interest rate policies and contributed to the recession that all Canadians have been affected by during the last year or so.
I shall return to that point shortly, but I also want to say that, prior to this budget, Canada has been a country in quite severe recession. That is in part the result of the failure of this government to take the five and six years of unprecedented prosperity in the 1980s as an occasion to rein in government spending, to make those years a real occasion of reducing the debt and reducing the deficit in accordance with all orthodox economic thinking.
After all, in past years, thanks in part to the measures of the Liberal government prior to 1984 introduced, we have had strong employment, strong economic output, strong income. Then there was a case for a more conservative fiscal policy. When the economy is buoyant that is the occasion to take measures to curtail in government spending and to permit the private sector to expand and develop as it can do in the circumstances which I have described.
But what we have seen is a reversal of Keynesian economics. We have had a reversal of orthodox economic thinking from this government. It did not act in a time of prosperity. It did not act during its first years in office to counter excessive spending in the economy. It did not rein in government spending. When the time came that it realized that the economy needed regulation and control, it sought only the monetary route to do so. It
The Budget
imposed ever higher interest rates on Canadians. It imposed interest rates as virtually its sole method of attempting to fight what it perceived as growing inflation in Canada. In doing so, it not only discouraged investment, discouraged small business, discouraged farmers from making further commitments to growth in our economy. But the government also increased, and I have to think intentionally, the spread between Canadian and U.S. interest rates to unprecedented levels. Now what does that mean for the average Canadian? It means a loss of jobs. It means a loss of exports. That is what the continuing wide gap between U.S. and Canadian interest rates means. Yet, this government went right ahead and persevered in its wrong-headed policy of ever-increasing interest rates.
The government knew that by doing so, that each point of increase in interest rates meant a yet higher deficit service charges for Canadians. Our deficit service charges increased until the point has been reached where the government has had to acknowledge in this budget that it has made no progress in reducing its deficits. Our deficit today is far higher than the Minister of Finance predicted only a year ago. It is back to what it was when he came into office following a major recession.
The result of this high interest rate policy and of the differences in interest rates between Canada and the United States has been to drive up the Canadian dollar. It has driven the Canadian dollar up to unrealistic levels, levels which do not match our productive capacity. The result of that unrealistic exchange rate is that we are suffering from the inability of Canadians to export not only to the United States, but abroad, because the value of the Canadian dollar is grossly inflated.
We have seen the results in Canada of the effect of the high interest rate policy the government has pursued with a wrong-headed obstinacy. If anyone does not believe what I am saying is reliable, let me refer to the Economic Council of Canada, a respected economic think tank financed by the government.
In reviewing economic policy of the past two years, the Council said that it does not believe that the current rate of unemployment is acceptable and unavoidable. The council concluded: "One painful lesson learned about fighting inflation with monetary restraint-that is, high interest rates-is that the remedy only works when it brings on a recession. This in turn reduces employment, investment and export sales". That is exactly what this government has done. It has brought on a made-in-Ca-

The Budget
nada recession. It has driven up unemployment. It has discouraged investment and our exports have sagged.
That is part of the background to the budget that the Minister of Finance introduced last night.
I want to turn for a moment to a more specific review of the minister's credibility. Last year in his budget, the Minister of Finance projected that interest rates would fall from 12 per cent in 1989 to 11 per cent in 1990. Instead, they averaged 13 per cent, further fueling the pressure on the deficit that I have already touched upon. As interest rates go up, so goes the deficit. The government has in response now cut and slashed programs in the name of reducing the deficit. Yet it created many of the circumstances, through high interest rates, that have lead to the major deficit that confronts every Canadian.
The Minister of Finance, in his last budget, predicted an inflation rate which would decline from 5 per cent in 1989 to 4.7 per cent in 1990 and would reach 4.5 per cent by the end of last year.
Yet, what is it today? Canada's inflation rate stands at 6.8 per cent although our economy has been enduring the made-in-Canada recession for over six months.
I want to cite another example of the inability of this Minister of Finance to offer the Canadian people accurate forecasts, accurate predictions, of what is going to happen in the economy in the time ahead.
The Minister of Finance's deficit prediction was $28.5 billion for 1990, and for 1991, $26.8 billion. Now we know that the deficit this past year has amounted to $30.5 billion and indeed the minister himself acknowledges that it would have been $35 billion if he had not acted in some way to reduce the growth in the deficit.
One can go on. There are many examples of how inaccurate this minister has been in his forecasting and in offering the Canadian people any certain guide to what lies ahead.
In his last budget, the minister predicted that Canada would experience a 1.2 per cent growth rate in 1990, but he added: "Growth is expected to rebound in the latter half of 1990 and in 1991, led by an improvement in net exports".
In fact, the economy shrank in the second quarter of 1990 by almost 2 percentage points to be followed by further contractions in both the third and fourth quarters of last year. Moreover, in the first quarter of 1990 I regret to say that Canada marked a record current account deficit in its trade of $20 billion. This was not the improvement in net exports which the Minister of Finance not a year ago promised the Canadian people.
What is the situation if we turn to the budget today? What is the situation with regard to the government's credibility and the Minister of Finance's forecasts?
This budget which is full of rhetoric but short of facts offers the assurance that short-term interest rates are expected to fall to 9.5 per cent this year from the current level of slightly over 10 per cent, and average 7 per cent over the medium term.
This is an interesting statement on the part of the Minister of Finance because until very recently he was as staunch a monetarist as the governor of the Bank of Canada. He was saying: "We must above all things pursue high interest rates as a method of restraining inflation". But suddenly the Minister of Finance seems to be a born-again fiscalist. He has given up his monetary obsessions and has now decided that the principal obstacle to increased affluence in Canada and increased prosperity is high interest rates. Above all things, we must now bring down interest rates.
Yet it was he himself who raised interest rates steadily every month, every month over the past year and a half. It is he who has now decided that his principal task is to bring down interest rates. But they are not to come down very much. They are just to come down from the current 10 per cent to a 9.5 per cent average over the next 12 months.
That is not much of a reduction. It certainly will do nothing to close the gap between Canadian and U.S. interest rates. It certainly will not be enough to bring about the resurgence of investment, the resurgence of economic commitment that all Canadians seek.
In believing that he can bring down interest rates even to that limited level, the Minister of Finance suggests that inflation will fall to 2.9 per cent by the end of 1992 and 2 per cent by 1995. Mr. Speaker, 2.9 per cent inflation by the end of 1992 from the 6 per cent and 5 per cent inflation that Canadians have been experiencing is a
February 27, 1991

major reduction. We are to see inflation cut in half in two years.
The Minister of Finance does not tell us how he is going to do this.
This is quite wonderful. This is quite marvellous. There is nothing that any of us would prefer to see than inflation brought down at such a rapid rate. But as the Toronto Globe and Mail said today, these numbers are amazing. They are not backed up by any information, any projections, any details about how Canada is to achieve this quite remarkable reduction in inflation while at the same time interest rates are only supposed to fall a very little bit.
The minister further claims in this budget that in 1992-93, instead of the present $30 billion-plus represented by the deficit, we shall have a deficit of $24 billion, $16 billion the following year, and $10 billion in 1994-95. These are amazing numbers, as the newspapers have said. But the Minister of Finance does not tell us how he is going to get there.
I would suggest that we take a very careful look at the assumptions made in this budget. The Canadian people will ask themselves where, for example, the 3.5 per cent growth is to come from next year. Canada, deep in a recession today and with some quarters exhibiting no growth and some quarters negative growth, suddenly next year is to achieve growth of 3.5 per cent and 4 per cent in the following year. The Minister of Finance, in offering these bald numbers unsubstantiated by any analysis, stretches the credulity of the Canadian people. Who can have confidence in these numbers on the basis of the minister's past performance or in the past performance of this government? These are numbers one might hope will be achieved, but on the present evidence
The Budget
and on past performance, the Canadian people can have no confidence that this government is capable of bringing about the radical change that is set forth in this budget. And yet, at what a price? At what price has the government set itself these goals?
The government talks about radically restructuring the economy, making Canada more competitive. What is most striking about the government's failure to act over the past seven years is that on the debt, on the underlying structural weaknesses in the economy, this government has not acted. It has not acted for seven years. It is now attempting to act in an inappropriate way. This is what comes from an economic philosophy that believes that the government has no role in the economy, in a political agenda which has resulted in the fragmentation of our country along regional, linguistic or social lines.
What the Canadian people are looking for are not these pie-in-the-sky, excessively optimistic, unsubstantiated budget measures which do not really address the principal issues confronting Canada today.
